discovery: Programmable arrays of individually trapped neutral atoms interacting via Rydberg blockade, for quantum simulation and entanglement of many particles

nominees.name: Antoine Browaeys
nominees.affiliation: Institut d'Optique Graduate School, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay, France

subfield: Atomic physics and quantum optics (quantum simulation)
motivation: The nominees made individual neutral atoms, held in optical tweezers and coupled through the Rydberg blockade, into a precise platform for building entanglement atom by atom. Lukin and colleagues proposed the dipole-blockade mechanism. In 2009 the Saffman and Browaeys groups first observed blockade between two single atoms and used it to entangle them. Browaeys and Lukin then built defect-free, reconfigurable arrays of hundreds of atoms. With these arrays they observed quantum magnetism, topological spin liquids and quantum many-body scars, and Lukin's team showed error-corrected logical qubits. These are clear, controlled experiments that pose sharp questions about many-body quantum physics and then answer them. They turn single-particle control and entanglement into a scalable tool, which is the core of the second quantum revolution, and their influence on quantum simulation and computing is already very large.
